title: Gendered experiences of living with multimorbidity in Malawi
content:
by Sangwani Nkhana Salimu, Stephen Anthony Spencer, Treighcy Banda, Marlen Chawani, Augustine Choko, Paul Dark, Julian Hertz, Blandina Mmbaga, Juma Mfinanga, Rhona Mijumbi, Adamson Sinjani Muula, Mulinda Nyirenda, Francis Sakita, Charity Salima, Hendry Sawe, Ibrahim Simiyu, Mirriam Taegtmeyer, Sarah Urasa, Nateiya Mmeta Yongolo, Jamie Rylance, Eve Worral, Felix Limbani, Deborah Nyirenda, Nicola Desmond, Ben Morton, MultiLink Consortium

Multimorbidity is an urgent public health problem in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). Gender influences healthcare access and health-seeking behaviours. The aim of this study was to examine gendered intersectional experiences of living with multimorbidity in Malawi. This qualitative study was nested within a broader program of multimorbidity research conducted at two hospitals in Malawi. We recruited patients with at least two of the following chronic conditions: diabetes, HIV, hypertension and chronic kidney disease. We conducted 32 in-depth-interviews (IDI) and 8 focus group discussions (FGDs) with PLWMM and their carers recruited at admission. Baseline data were supplemented with follow-up interviews at 90 days post-hospital admission to capture evolving experiences, self-management, and care-seeking. Data were analysed thematically using critical gender theory. Four key themes emerged: gendered perceptions of chronic conditions; gendered engagement with medical pluralism, unspoken depression; gendered roles and care-seeking; and decision-making. Experiences were shaped by intersecting factors including gender norms, age, household power dynamics, disease type, and socio-economic status. Men, particularly younger and economically active, experienced stress linked to reduced physical capacity, inability to fulfil provider roles, and concerns about sexual health. Across both genders, limited access to resources and declining functionality influenced self-management and engagement with care. Women were more likely to engage in complementary treatments, influenced by caregiving roles and household economic constraints, while men predominantly focused on managing treatment side-effects and maintaining social roles. Gendered experiences of multimorbidity in Malawi are shaped by broader social, cultural and economic inequalities. Multimorbidity care should adopt intersectionality-informed and gender-responsive approaches that strengthen patient-centred communication, social support, and equitable access to care.
